q: You're driving on a motorway at 70 mph in good, dry conditions. What is the typical overall stopping distance?
options: 53 metres (175 feet)
73 metres (240 feet)
96 metres (315 feet)
36 metres (118 feet)
explain: At 70 mph on a dry road the typical overall stopping distance is 96 metres (315 feet): 21 metres thinking distance plus 75 metres braking distance. That's about twenty-four car lengths.

q: You're driving along a dry street with a 30 mph speed limit. What is the typical overall stopping distance at 30 mph?
options: 12 metres
36 metres
9 metres
23 metres
explain: At 30 mph the typical overall stopping distance is 23 metres (75 feet): 9 metres thinking distance plus 14 metres braking distance, or about six car lengths.

q: You're driving at 50 mph on a dry road when a hazard appears ahead. What is the typical thinking distance at this speed?
options: 15 metres
12 metres
38 metres
18 metres
explain: At 50 mph the typical thinking distance is 15 metres. The braking distance adds a further 38 metres, giving a typical overall stopping distance of 53 metres (175 feet).

q: You're travelling at 60 mph on a dry single carriageway. What is the typical braking distance at this speed, not counting thinking distance?
options: 73 metres
55 metres
38 metres
18 metres
explain: At 60 mph the typical braking distance is 55 metres. Add the 18 metres thinking distance and the typical overall stopping distance is 73 metres (240 feet).

q: You're driving at 40 mph on a dry road. What is the typical overall stopping distance?
options: 23 metres
24 metres
36 metres
53 metres
explain: At 40 mph the typical overall stopping distance is 36 metres (118 feet): 12 metres thinking distance plus 24 metres braking distance, or about nine car lengths.

q: You're on a dry dual carriageway at 60 mph. Taking an average car length as 4 metres, about how many car lengths is your typical overall stopping distance?
options: Nine
Thirteen
Twenty-four
Eighteen
explain: At 60 mph the typical overall stopping distance is 73 metres (240 feet), or about eighteen car lengths. The safe rule is never to get closer than the overall stopping distance to the vehicle in front.

q: The Highway Code's typical stopping distances are only a general guide. Which factor does it say your thinking distance depends on?
options: The condition of your brakes
The road surface
Your attention
The type of tyres fitted
explain: The stopping distances diagram says the distance will depend on your attention (thinking distance), the road surface, the weather conditions and the condition of your vehicle at the time.

q: You're following another car on a fast road. What does the Highway Code give as the safe rule for how close you should get?
options: Never closer than the typical braking distance
Never closer than the overall stopping distance
Never closer than the typical thinking distance
Never closer than three car lengths away
explain: Leave enough space to pull up safely if the vehicle in front suddenly slows down or stops. The safe rule is never to get closer than the overall stopping distance.

q: You're driving on a dry, high-speed road. What is the minimum time gap you should leave between you and the vehicle in front?
options: One second
Half a second
Four seconds
Two seconds
explain: You should allow at least a two-second gap on high-speed roads and in tunnels where visibility is reduced. Use a fixed point, such as a sign, to help you measure it.

q: It's raining and you're driving on a dual carriageway. In the dry you'd leave a two-second gap. What gap should you now leave?
options: At least four seconds
About three seconds
Two seconds is still enough
About one second
explain: The two-second gap should be at least doubled on wet roads. In wet weather stopping distances will be at least double those on dry roads, because your tyres have less grip.

q: You're driving on an icy road. Compared with a dry road, how much greater might your gap from the vehicle in front need to be?
options: Up to twice as great
Up to ten times greater
Up to four times greater
About the same
explain: The gap should be up to ten times greater on icy roads. Stopping distances can be ten times greater than on dry roads, so keep well back from the road user in front.

q: You're driving through a tunnel and the traffic ahead comes to a stop. What is the minimum gap you should leave between you and the vehicle in front?
options: 2 metres
10 metres
5 metres
20 metres
explain: If you have to stop in a tunnel, leave at least a 5-metre gap between you and the vehicle in front. While moving, allow at least a two-second gap, as visibility in tunnels is reduced.

q: Your passenger says the driver behind you is tailgating. What does tailgating mean?
options: Driving with the rear fog lights on
Overtaking a vehicle on its left
Towing a trailer that sways
Following too closely to stop safely
explain: Tailgating is where the gap between you and the vehicle in front is too small for you to stop safely if it suddenly brakes. It's dangerous, intimidating and can cause collisions, especially at speed.

q: You're keeping a safe gap on a dual carriageway when another driver overtakes and pulls into the space in front of you. What should you do?
options: Close up so nobody else cuts in
Flash your headlights at the driver
Drop back to regain a two-second gap
Overtake the driver again
explain: If someone overtakes and pulls into the gap in front of you, drop back to maintain a two-second gap. Never speed up or obstruct a driver who is overtaking you.

q: You're driving in heavy rain behind a lorry. Why should you keep well back from it?
options: To stop your brakes from getting wet
To see and plan further ahead
To let your tyres warm up and grip
To stop your wipers from overloading
explain: In wet weather you should keep well back from the vehicle in front. This will increase your ability to see and plan ahead, as rain and spray from vehicles may make it difficult to see and be seen.

q: You're driving through heavy rain when the steering suddenly feels unresponsive. What should you do?
options: Ease off and slow down gradually
Brake hard to slow down quickly
Steer sharply to regain grip
Accelerate to get through the water
explain: If the steering becomes unresponsive in wet weather, it probably means that water is preventing the tyres from gripping the road. Ease off the accelerator and slow down gradually.

q: You're driving on a wet road and pass a fuel station. Why should you be aware of spilt diesel on the road?
options: It makes your brakes overheat
It damages your tyre sidewalls
It causes your engine to stall
It makes the road very slippery
explain: Spilt diesel makes the road surface very slippery, as it significantly reduces the grip between tyres and the road. It's especially dangerous for motorcyclists.

q: The local forecast warns of snow and ice overnight. You'd planned to drive somewhere the next morning. What should you do?
options: Drive as normal once the roads are gritted
Drive only if your journey is essential
Lower your tyre pressures for extra grip
Follow other vehicles' tracks closely
explain: Don't drive in icy or snowy weather unless your journey is essential. If it is, take great care, allow more time and drive with care even if the roads have been treated.

q: You have to drive on a road that is icy. Which of these is the safest way to drive?
options: Slowly, in the lowest gear possible
At a steady speed in neutral
Slowly, in as high a gear as possible
Briskly, to spend less time on the ice
explain: When the roads are icy, drive at a slow speed in as high a gear as possible, and accelerate and brake very gently. Avoid sudden actions, as these could cause loss of control.

q: You're approaching a bend on an icy road. When should you do your braking?
options: On the straight before the bend
As you start to steer into the bend
Halfway round the bend
As you leave the bend
explain: Drive particularly slowly on bends, where loss of control is more likely. Brake progressively on the straight before you reach the bend, then steer smoothly round it, avoiding sudden actions.

q: It's a freezing winter night and you notice your tyres are making almost no noise on the road. What could this mean?
options: The road is wet with rain
Your tyres are under-inflated
You're driving on ice
The road has just been gritted
explain: When travelling on ice, tyres make virtually no noise. Steering that feels unresponsive may also mean ice, and that your vehicle is losing its grip on the road.

q: You're following a snowplough on a dual carriageway. When could you consider overtaking it?
options: When the lane you'll use has been cleared
As soon as it slows down for a junction
When it moves into the left-hand lane
Whenever there's a long, clear straight
explain: Snowploughs may throw out snow on either side. Don't overtake them unless the lane you intend to use has been cleared.

q: What usually causes a car to skid?
options: Braking early and lightly before bends
Keeping to a steady speed on the straight
Steering smoothly on a dry, level road
Harsh braking, accelerating or steering
explain: Skidding is usually caused by the driver braking, accelerating or steering too harshly, or driving too fast for the road conditions.

q: You're driving on a slippery road and the rear of your car skids to the right. What should you do?
options: Steer to the left
Brake firmly
Steer to the right
Pull the handbrake on
explain: Turn the steering wheel in the direction of the skid. If the rear of the vehicle skids to the right, steer immediately to the right to recover.

q: You brake too harshly on a wet bend and your car starts to skid. What should you do to remove the cause?
options: Press the brake pedal harder
Release the brake pedal fully
Apply the handbrake as well
Switch off the engine
explain: If skidding occurs, remove the cause by releasing the brake pedal fully or easing off the accelerator. Then steer in the direction of the skid.

q: Your car has anti-lock brakes (ABS) and you have to stop in an emergency. How should you use the footbrake?
options: Press firmly and keep the pressure on
Pump it on and off rapidly
Press gently, then use the handbrake
Press firmly, then release it quickly
explain: In an emergency, apply the footbrake firmly and don't release the pressure until the vehicle has slowed to the desired speed. Otherwise, follow the advice in your vehicle handbook.

q: You're driving a car fitted with anti-lock brakes on a wet road. What should you remember?
options: ABS lets you follow more closely
ABS may not shorten your stopping distance
ABS halves stopping distances in the wet
ABS stops the tyres losing grip in water
explain: ABS should help you keep steering control, but don't assume a vehicle with ABS will stop in a shorter distance. On wet roads your gap should be at least doubled.

q: You've just driven through deep water and your brakes don't feel fully effective. What should you do?
options: Brake hard several times at speed
Pump the handbrake on and off
Drive fast to blow the water off
Brake lightly while driving slowly
explain: After driving through deep water your brakes may be less effective. If they're not fully effective, gently apply light pressure while driving slowly. This will help to dry them out.

q: You're driving along a dual carriageway and can see a bank of fog ahead. What should you do before you enter it?
options: Check your mirrors, then slow down
Speed up to get through it quickly
Brake sharply to warn drivers behind
Switch on your hazard warning lights
explain: Before entering fog, check your mirrors, then slow down. Even if fog seems to be clearing, you can suddenly find yourself in thick fog.

q: You pass a sign showing 'Fog', but the road ahead looks clear. What should you do?
options: Ignore it, as the fog must have cleared
Switch on your rear fog lights straight away
Be prepared for a bank of fog ahead
Speed up to get past the area quickly
explain: If 'Fog' is shown on a sign but the road is clear, be prepared for a bank of fog or drifting patchy fog ahead. Only use fog lights when visibility is seriously reduced.

q: You're driving on a motorway in fog. What speed should you be driving at?
options: Fast enough to keep up with the traffic around you
Slow enough to stop in the distance you can see
Fast enough to keep the lights ahead in view
Close to the limit so you aren't hit from behind
explain: In fog you should be able to pull up well within the distance you can see clearly. This is particularly important on motorways and dual carriageways, as vehicles are travelling faster.

q: You MUST use headlights when visibility is seriously reduced. What does 'seriously reduced' generally mean?
options: You can't see for more than 200 metres
You can't see for more than 300 metres
You can't see for more than 500 metres
You can't see for more than 100 metres
explain: You MUST use headlights when visibility is seriously reduced, generally when you can't see for more than 100 metres (328 feet). You may also use fog lights, but you MUST switch them off when visibility improves.

q: You've been using your front and rear fog lights in thick fog. The fog has now cleared. What MUST you do?
options: Switch them off
Leave them on until you park
Switch off only the front ones
Leave only the rear ones on
explain: You MUST switch fog lights off when visibility improves. They dazzle other road users and can obscure your brake lights.

q: It's a very windy day. Which type of vehicle is most affected by the wind?
options: High-sided vehicles
Large saloon cars
Low sports cars
Four-wheel-drive cars
explain: High-sided vehicles are most affected by windy weather, but strong gusts can also blow a car, cyclist, motorcyclist or horse rider off course.

q: You're driving on a windy day. Where are strong gusts most likely to blow you off course?
options: In a sheltered residential street
On an open stretch of road
In a queue of slow-moving traffic
In a multi-storey car park
explain: Strong gusts can blow vehicles off course on open stretches of road exposed to strong crosswinds, or when passing bridges or gaps in hedges.

q: It's very windy. Ahead of you, a motorcyclist is overtaking a high-sided lorry. What should you do?
options: Stay close behind the motorcyclist
Overtake the motorcyclist straight away
Sound your horn to warn the rider
Keep well back from the motorcyclist
explain: In very windy weather, turbulence created by large vehicles can affect other road users. Motorcyclists are particularly affected, so keep well back from them when they're overtaking a high-sided vehicle.

q: You're about to overtake a cyclist on a day with strong winds. How much room should you give them?
options: Less than usual so you pass quickly
More than you would in calm weather
The same as you'd give a parked car
Just enough to clear their handlebars
explain: Take extra care and give more space when overtaking cyclists, motorcyclists and horse riders in bad weather, including high winds, and at night. Gusts can blow them off course.

q: It starts to rain after a long spell of hot, dry weather. What should you be aware of?
options: Your tyres will grip better
Your brakes will work better
The road may become slippery
Your stopping distance will shorten
explain: If it rains after a dry spell, the road surface may become slippery. This could affect your steering and braking.

q: You're on a long drive on a very hot day. Why should you keep your car well ventilated?
options: To avoid becoming drowsy
To stop the tyres overheating
To keep the brakes cool
To stop the engine overheating
explain: In hot weather, keep your vehicle well ventilated to avoid drowsiness. If you're dazzled by bright sunlight, slow down and, if necessary, stop.

q: Your driving instructor warns you not to coast. What does 'coasting' mean?
options: Slowing down by changing to a lower gear
Driving at a steady speed in top gear
Travelling in neutral or with the clutch down
Following close behind another vehicle
explain: Coasting describes a vehicle travelling in neutral or with the clutch pressed down. It can reduce your control because engine braking is eliminated.

q: You're driving down a steep hill. Why is it dangerous to coast in neutral?
options: Your speed will increase quickly
Your engine may overheat
Your fuel use will rise sharply
Your tyres will wear unevenly
explain: Coasting eliminates engine braking, so your speed downhill will increase quickly. It can also affect steering response and make it harder to select the right gear when you need it.

q: You're following a large lorry and would like to overtake it. Why should you drop back?
options: So you can build up speed before pulling out
So the lorry driver can speed up
So you can overtake on the left if needed
So you can see further ahead and be seen
explain: Dropping back increases your ability to see ahead and should allow the driver of the large vehicle to see you in their mirrors. Getting too close will obscure your view of the road ahead.

q: You're behind a car that pulls out to overtake a long lorry. You also want to overtake the lorry. What should you do?
options: Follow the car closely as it passes
Pull out alongside the car to pass together
Wait, as the car may abort and pull back in
Flash your headlights to hurry the car
explain: Don't assume you can follow a vehicle ahead that is overtaking a long vehicle. If a problem develops, they may abort the overtake and pull back in.

q: You're about to overtake a cyclist on a road with a 30 mph limit. As a guide, what is the minimum space you should leave?
options: 75 centimetres
1 metre
50 centimetres
1.5 metres
explain: As a guide, leave at least 1.5 metres when overtaking cyclists at speeds of up to 30 mph, and give them more space when overtaking at higher speeds.

q: You're driving along a country road and see a horse rider ahead. How should you pass them?
options: Below 20 mph, leaving at least 1 metre
Below 10 mph, leaving at least 2 metres
Below 30 mph, leaving at least 1.5 metres
Below 15 mph, leaving at least 1 metre
explain: Pass horse riders and horse-drawn vehicles at speeds under 10 mph and allow at least 2 metres of space. Always pass wide and slowly.

q: You're about to overtake a motorcyclist on a single carriageway. How much room should you give them?
options: Less than you'd give a car
Just enough to clear their mirror
Half the width of your lane
At least as much as you'd give a car
explain: Give motorcyclists, cyclists, horse riders and horse-drawn vehicles at least as much room as you would when overtaking a car.

q: You're following a cyclist on a narrow, winding road. There isn't room to pass with a safe gap. What should you do?
options: Wait behind until it's safe to pass
Pass slowly, leaving less space
Sound your horn so they move in
Flash your headlights to warn them
explain: You should wait behind the cyclist and not overtake if it's unsafe or not possible to give them the recommended space.

q: You're approaching the start of a contraflow system at road works. Why should you slow down and increase your distance from the vehicle in front?
options: The lanes will be wider than normal
Changes in road camber may affect stability
Speed cameras are only used at the start
The road surface will always be wet
explain: In a contraflow you may be in a narrower lane than normal with no permanent barrier between you and oncoming traffic. At the start and finish, slow down and increase your distance from the vehicle in front, as changes in camber may affect vehicle stability.

q: You're driving through road works where the lanes are narrower than normal. What should you do?
options: Overtake queuing traffic to get through
Keep close to the vehicle in front
Keep a safe distance and watch the lane edges
Straddle the lanes to give yourself room
explain: Narrow lanes at road works are marked by studs or temporary road markings. Keep a safe distance from the vehicle in front and make sure you can clearly see the edges of the lane ahead.

q: You're driving through road works with grit and mud on the road surface. Which road users are most at risk of skidding?
options: Drivers of large lorries
Cyclists and motorcyclists
Drivers of buses and coaches
Drivers of four-wheel-drive cars
explain: Take extra care near cyclists and motorcyclists at road works, as they are vulnerable to skidding on grit, mud or other debris.
